query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In initially homogeneous single‐phase high-entropy alloys, controlled thermal aging combined with mechanical loading induces nanoscale elemental segregation at grain boundaries. This segregation forms localized clusters that reduce interfacial cohesion and promote brittle behavior, even though the alloy remains macroscopically single-phase—an effect distinct from the extensive grain-boundary precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy with uniformly distributed constituent elements.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging at service-relevant temperatures combined with mechanical loading.
generation.conditions: Service-like high temperatures that activate diffusion and mechanical loading near operational stress thresholds.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary regions developing nanoscale segregated clusters.
generation.mechanism: Differential diffusion under service conditions leads to local chemical inhomogeneities at grain boundaries. This initiates the formation of nanoscale clusters that diminish grain-boundary cohesion, thereby facilitating crack nucleation and brittle fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a rapidly quenched, homogenized baseline sample, thermally aged and mechanically loaded samples will exhibit reduced toughness (e.g., lower fracture toughness and impact energy absorption) along with microstructural evidence of nanoscale segregation at grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: A homogenized single-phase high-entropy alloy processed by rapid quenching to prevent grain-boundary segregation.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to be active under service conditions where temperatures and stresses are sufficient to activate diffusion. At very low temperatures or under minimal loading, the diffusion-driven segregation and resulting brittleness are not expected to occur.
generation.uncertainty: The absolute magnitude of toughness reduction and the extent of segregation may depend on specific alloy compositions and precise service conditions, which warrants further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to thermal aging at service-relevant temperatures combined with controlled mechanical loading, while maintaining the other set as a rapidly quenched, homogenized baseline. Use high-resolution microscopy techniques (e.g., TEM, atom probe tomography) to assess grain-boundary chemistry and segregation, and perform standardized fracture toughness and impact tests on both sets.
measurements: Impact energy (e.g., via Charpy or drop-weight tests)
Microstructural characterization (TEM, atom probe tomography) to detect nanoscale grain-boundary segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged and loaded samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in toughness and no measurable nanoscale grain-boundary segregation relative to the rapidly quenched baseline, then the hypothesis that diffusion-induced nanoscale segregation causes brittle behavior is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior emerges from local nanoscale elemental segregation at grain boundaries induced by service conditions that trigger limited, incipient intermetallic (or structurally brittle) clustering—a mechanism that is distinct from the more extensive grain-boundary precipitation observed in conventional alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with compositionally complex but uniformly distributed elements.
drafts.intervention: Application of controlled thermal aging at service-relevant temperatures combined with mechanical loading to stimulate diffusion‐driven segregation.
drafts.conditions: Service-like high temperatures (where diffusion becomes active) and representative mechanical loading (e.g., impact or fatigue tests) that approach operational stress thresholds.
drafts.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary regions that develop nanoscale segregated clusters, which may serve as precursors to brittle intermetallic or structurally anisotropic zones.
drafts.mechanism: Under service conditions, differential diffusion among constituent elements leads to local chemical inhomogeneities at grain boundaries. This subtle segregation precipitates the formation of brittle clusters that reduce interfacial cohesive strength and facilitate crack nucleation, promoting brittle fracture behavior even though the alloy remains macroscopically single phase.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline single-phase HEA with quenched (retained homogeneity) treatment, thermally aged samples will exhibit lower toughness (e.g., reduced fracture toughness, lower impact energy absorption) and show microstructural evidence of nanoscale segregation at grain boundaries. This pattern is distinct from conventional alloys where brittle behavior is more directly linked to extensive grain-boundary precipitation.
drafts.baseline: A compositionally complex HEA processed to ensure uniform elemental distribution with no detectable grain-boundary segregation (e.g., via rapid quenching or other homogenization techniques).
drafts.boundary: Service-relevant temperatures and mechanical stresses at which diffusion is sufficient to enable grain-boundary segregation; outside these conditions (e.g., at very low temperatures or under very low stress) the mechanism may not activate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to thermal aging under service-like temperatures and controlled mechanical loading; treat the other set with rapid quenching to preserve homogenous microstructures. Use high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM and atom probe tomography) to assess grain-boundary chemistry and segregation, and perform standardized fracture toughness and impact tests on both sets.
measurements: Impact energy from Charpy or drop-weight tests
Microstructural characterization (TEM, atom probe tomography) focused on detecting nanoscale segregation at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show statistically significant reductions in toughness (or an increase in brittle fracture behavior) and no detectable grain-boundary segregation relative to the rapidly-quenched baseline, then the hypothesized mechanism of segregation-induced brittleness is falsified.
